summary:
The statutory baseline in Austria is permissive. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016. The Equal Treatment Act has covered employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2004, and recent amendments have broadened its use of "gender" to encompass gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; every federal state extended anti-discrimination protection to goods and services by January 2017, Lower Austria being the last to do so.

Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1 January 2016, and offences committed on that ground are treated as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The 1993 Security Police Act obliges police to avoid actions that could be perceived as biased on grounds of sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition is available without mandatory sex-reassignment surgery, and Austrian documents may carry an "X", an indeterminate marker or no marker at all; intersex people may choose "divers", "inter" or no designation. A significant restriction qualifies that framework. Following the Constitutional Court's June 2018 ruling that official documents must reflect gender identity accurately, Austria issued its first "X" passport and "divers" birth certificate in 2019 to intersex activist Alex Jürgen, but the Interior Ministry limited "divers" registration to applicants holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality. A name and legal gender change is conditional on submission of a psychiatric opinion, and public health insurance payment for gender-related treatment is likewise bound to psychiatric opinions.

Violence risk is documented and specific. In March 2025 police uncovered a neo-Nazi network that used fake dating-platform profiles to lure gay and bisexual men to remote locations, where masked assailants ambushed and filmed them and circulated the footage. Austrian police arrested 15 people aged 14 to 26 over the wave of attacks; at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured in this way and then falsely accused of being paedophiles, and investigators believe the real victim count is substantially higher.

Official recording gives scale to the pattern. Austria registered 6,751 suspected hate crimes and 7,327 prejudice motives in 2025, including 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, with police and monitoring bodies acknowledging under-recording. Reporting on the same figures shows homophobic offences rising while transphobic incidents declined over the reporting year.

Detention carries its own set of rules. A 2025 Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report, produced within an EU-funded project, sets out the legal framework governing LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons and their rights in detention, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection, and the Justice Ministry answered parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 in May and June 2025 on official rules for housing transgender people in penal institutions. That answer is the authority to cite if a trans visitor is detained, and it is published in German.

Care access is supported at professional level: the Austrian Society of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and the Austrian Society of Gynecology and Obstetrics have endorsed puberty blockers for young people experiencing gender dysphoria. Public administration has moved toward inclusion in lower-stakes settings, with Ombuds guidance issued on gender-inclusive forms for intersex and non-binary people.
tangentialFactors:
Political turbulence forms part of the context. The far-right Freedom Party won the most votes in a national election for the first time since the Second World War in September 2024, taking 29.2% of the vote, which prompted concern among LGBTQ observers about what an FPÖ-led government would mean for LGBTQ people. The ÖVP and FPÖ have historically opposed LGBT rights legislation.

The 2025 reporting year also produced administrative friction adjacent to queer life: the Ministry of Education introduced rules restricting outside sex-education providers, and a Vienna petition requesting dedicated queer sauna time slots was rejected.

Public opinion runs well ahead of the loudest political rhetoric. Polling as of 2023 showed 65% support for same-sex marriage and 66% agreeing that there is nothing wrong with a same-sex relationship, and political visibility is high, with seven openly gay National Council politicians after the 2019 election and the first openly LGBT government minister appointed in June 2019.

Historical comparison is stark: prosecutions were harsh under earlier regimes, with lesbianism criminalised after the Anschluss and 1940 court alignment to Paragraph 175, and as of July 2020 no expungement or compensation scheme for those historical convictions had been implemented.
localsOnly:
Transgender Austrians can change legal gender and name without prior sex-reassignment surgery, but the change requires a psychiatric opinion, and the same condition attaches to insurance payment for gender-related treatment. Intersex and non-binary applicants seeking the "divers" designation must present a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

Open service in the Austrian Armed Forces has been permitted for all personnel, transgender people included, since 2014. Advocacy operates openly through organisations such as HOSI Wien, founded 1979, HOSI Salzburg, ALGF and Afro Rainbow Austria, with community infrastructure in Vienna, Linz, Innsbruck, Salzburg and Graz and an annual Vienna Pride parade.

Conversion therapy remains unresolved in statute. The National Council passed a non-binding resolution on 2 July 2019 calling for a government bill banning conversion therapy on minors, carried with all parties voting in favour, after the ultra-conservative association TeenSTAR was found in 2018 offering minors classes teaching that sexual orientation is changeable. The Education Directorate Salzburg banned TeenSTAR workshops pending review and the association itself was banned in April 2019, but no binding statutory ban is recorded in these sources.

Lesbian couples can access artificial insemination and IVF treatment. Sources note that many LGBT people still regard being different as a problem, a sentiment attributed to Catholic influence on public attitudes.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules are not covered by the source inventory, so whether a trans visitor's documents are examined for gender-marker consistency on arrival is unresolved here rather than answered.

It is not established in these sources whether the Interior Ministry's intersex-certificate limit on the "divers" designation still stands in its 2019 form, or whether later practice has widened it; the restriction is documented as of the 2019 reporting, and the March 2026 overview does not restate its current status.

The psychiatric-opinion condition on legal gender change is reported in country coverage whose overall date is not specified, so its present applicability alongside the stated position that no mandatory medical procedure is required is unresolved.

Neither the prison housing rules nor the Ludwig Boltzmann report's findings on placement outcomes are summarised here beyond their scope: the Justice Ministry answer is German-language and was not read into this record, and no data on how often trans detainees are housed in accordance with their gender identity appears in the inventory.

Hate-crime figures are reported alongside explicit acknowledgement of under-recording, and the split between rising homophobic and declining transphobic offences is not accompanied by absolute transphobic counts, so the direction of that change cannot be quantified from these sources.
